dogmatic

dawg-MAT-ik -- from Greek dogma, 'opinion, belief,' from dokein, 'to think, to seem': a dogmatic person treats one opinion as beyond question. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Dogmatic is rigidly uncompromising about one's own principles or beliefs.

No amount of new evidence could move the committee's most dogmatic member off his original position.

Example

Even after three separate studies contradicted his original claim, the dogmatic researcher continued presenting it at conferences exactly as before, refusing to revise a single sentence of his argument.

Dogmatic describes someone who treats their own belief as beyond question -- ignoring three separate contradicting studies rather than adjusting the claim even slightly is exactly that kind of rigid certainty.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

stubborn: Stubborn means refusing to budge -- about a route, a bedtime, an apology, anything. It is about will rather than ideas. Dogmatic is narrower and sharper: it targets beliefs and principles, treating them as beyond question. A stubborn person will not move; a dogmatic one will not rethink.

preachy: Preachy criticizes the delivery: someone who keeps lecturing others about how to think or live, whatever they actually believe underneath. Dogmatic criticizes the mind itself -- principles held as unquestionable no matter the evidence. A preachy friend moralizes at you; a dogmatic one cannot imagine being wrong.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

open-minded: willing to consider new ideas or arguments

flexible: willing to change or adapt

Where it sits · how closed the mind stays — opinionated → dogmatic → inflexible

opinionated vs. dogmatic: Opinionated simply means holding strong views and stating them often, while dogmatic adds the sharper criticism that someone refuses to even entertain the possibility they're wrong.

inflexible vs. dogmatic: Inflexible pushes further than dogmatic by emphasizing total rigidity in any situation, not just a refusal to update one particular belief.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — dogmat

Root — dogmat: opinion, belief (Greek dogma, whose stem is dogmat-, from dokein 'to think, to seem')

Suffix — -ic

Suffix — -ic: characteristic of (Greek -ikos)

Put it together

Put it together: Dogmat ('opinion, belief' -- Greek dogma, whose stem is dogmat-, from dokein 'to think, to seem') + -ic ('characteristic of') spell dogmatic: treating one's own opinion as unquestionable doctrine. The same ancient root dokein sits, more distantly, inside orthodox -- orthos ('straight, right') plus doxa ('opinion').

Use the root in a new word: orthodox

Use the root in a new word: orthodox: The chef trained for years in classic, orthodox French technique before inventing his own style.
